paragraphs.text: Additionally, unlike in the case of the non-GNN deep neural networks [4,6,7], the existing QGNNs do not leverage the quaternion space to reduce the number of parameters. In these non-GNN methods, the input features are usually divided in such a way that overall the four components of the quaternion vector can aggregate them and make a meaningful transformation out of it. The previous work [8], however, uses each quaternion component to work with all the features. This adds four times the computational overhead, making the model expensive in terms of training and inference time. Additionally, it makes the outputs very sensitive to even a tiny change in the input, as this type of quaternion GNN amplifies the tiny change. To this end, we restrict our quaternion model from quadrupling the number of parameters, thereby reducing the trainable parameter count to one-fourth of that of real, and this also prohibits the output from being extremely sensitive to the tiny change in the input features.

In this work, our goal is to attain Quaternion Graph Neural Networks that are expressive and have fewer parameters. To do this, we first propose a generic framework to get the Quaternion model corresponding to any GNN model with real representations. Secondly, we present a framework to sparsify the Quater- nion GNNs so that we reduce the number of parameters by finding a lottery ticket. We generalize the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis [2] to Quaternion Graph Neural Networks. For graphs, the existing unified graph lottery ticket, which prunes the input graph as well as the GNN to obtain the winning graph lottery ticket, has some drawbacks. Primarily, it is not feasible to prune the input graph along with the GNNs in graph-level tasks. UGS lacks effectiveness for transfer learning purposes because of its dependency on the input graph. We tackle this by redefining the lottery ticket for graphs. Figure 1 presents an overview of our approach.

To summarize, this paper makes contributions as follows: (1) Quaternion Message Passing Neural Networks (QMPNNs): We present a generalizable frame- work for computing quaternion space representations using any GNN, reducing trainable parameters by 75%. (2) We redefine the graph lottery tickets from a

Fig. 1: Pruning a quaternion message passing neural network. Graph's features are first transformed into quaternion features. We train QMPNN, which has quaternion weights, for the given task. Furthermore, to find our proposed winning lottery ticket, we prune and train the QMPNN until we get a model with pruned quaternion weights that gives a comparable accuracy. The pruned quaternion network can be trained with only a small fraction of the parameters in the real GNN.

different perspective for GNNs and QMPNNs. (3) To our knowledge, we are the first to empirically demonstrate the existence of graph lottery tickets in QMPNNs. (4) We provide the performance evaluation of the proposed LTH on both GNNs and QMPNNs on real-world datasets for three graph-based tasks - node classification, link prediction, and graph classification.

## 2 Background
### 2.1 Notations and Definitions
We use the following notations in this paper. A graph $\mathcal{G} = \{\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E}\}$ has a set of vertices $\mathcal{V}$ and a set of edges $\mathcal{E}$. The feature vector corresponding to a node $v \in \mathcal{V}$ is given as $\mathrm{x}_v$ in $\mathbb{R}^F$. The feature matrix for the graph is given as $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}| \times F}$. The edge $e_{ij} = (v_i, v_j) \in \mathcal{E}$ if and only if there is an edge between two nodes $v_i$ and $v_j$. In the adjacency matrix representation $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}| \times |\mathcal{V}|}$ of the graph, the $\mathbf{A}_{ij} = 1$ if $e_{ij} \in \mathcal{E}$, and 0 otherwise.

related_claims.content: Winning graph-lottery tickets exist for both real-valued GNNs and QMPNNs.
the quaternion reparameterization is effective on large-scale graph benchmarks.

Representing layer weights as quaternion matrices and grouping four real feature channels into one quaternion reduces the number of independent trainable real parameters by a factor of four relative to an equivalent real-valued GNN weight matrix.

A quaternion weight mapping from $F$ real input features to $F'$ real outputs uses $F/4\times F'/4$ quaternion entries, yielding one-fourth the degrees of freedom of the corresponding real weight matrix.

The parameter reduction described in claim 2 is achieved without increasing matrix-multiplication time complexity. [Referenced claim 2: Representing layer weights as quaternion matrices and grouping four real feature channels into one quaternion reduces the number of independent trainable real parameters by a factor of four relative to an equivalent real-valued GNN weight matrix.]

The MESSAGE, AGGREGATE, and UPDATE functions of any message-passing GNN are replaced by their quaternion counterparts so that the layerwise message-passing semantics are preserved in quaternion space.
QMPNN variants scale to large graph datasets and maintain performance comparable to real-valued GNNs while using fewer parameters.

Across all tasks and datasets evaluated, quaternion variants of standard GNN architectures frequently perform within a small margin of the corresponding real models and sometimes exceed their performance while consistently having approximately one-fourth the trainable parameter count of the corresponding real models.
Quaternion matrix multiplications have the same asymptotic time complexity as the corresponding real matrix multiplications.

When QMPNN variants of standard GNN architectures are trained under the same hyperparameters as those standard GNN architectures and evaluated on standard datasets, the quaternion models achieve comparable or better accuracy, ROC-AUC, or Hits@K (proportion of top-K predictions that are correct) while using roughly one-fourth of the trainable parameters of those standard GNN architectures.

When the three QMPNN variants QGCN, QGAT, and QSAGE of standard GNN architectures are trained under the same hyperparameters as those standard GNN architectures and evaluated on standard datasets, the quaternion models achieve comparable or better accuracy, ROC-AUC, or Hits@K (proportion of top-K predictions that are correct) while using roughly one-fourth of the trainable parameters of those standard GNN architectures.
